hints: Count the number of bonding pairs and lone pairs around the central atom in $\text{AlCl}_3$ and $\text{PCl}_3$ by looking at their Group numbers and outer electrons.
Recall how a lone pair changes the arrangement, compare a central atom with 3 bonding pairs only versus 3 bonding pairs plus 1 lone pair.
Think of the ideal angles for 3 electron domains in a plane versus a tetrahedral arrangement with one position taken by a lone pair.
Remember how to show 3D shape on paper, flat arrangement for one molecule and wedge or hashed bonds plus a lone pair for the other.
walkthrough:
Work out the electron domains on aluminium**
Al is in Group 13, so it has 3 outer electrons. In $\text{AlCl}_3$ it forms 3 bonding pairs with Cl and has no lone pair left. That gives 3 electron domains, all bonding. They repel equally, so they spread as far apart as possible in one plane.

Name the AlCl3 shape and angle**
Three bonding pairs with no lone pair always gives trigonal planar. The three $\text{Cl-Al-Cl}$ angles are equal: $$\text{bond angle} = 120^{\circ}$$ Draw Al in the centre with three straight lines to Cl at $120^{\circ}$ to each other, all in the plane of the paper.

Work out the electron domains on phosphorus**
P is in Group 15, so it has 5 outer electrons. In $\text{PCl}_3$ it forms 3 bonding pairs with Cl, leaving one lone pair on P. That gives 4 electron domains in total, 3 bonding plus 1 lone pair. The basic electron arrangement is tetrahedral, but the shape seen is decided by atom positions only.

Name the PCl3 shape and angle**
Three bonding pairs plus one lone pair gives trigonal pyramidal. The lone pair repels more strongly than bonding pairs, so it squeezes the $\text{Cl-P-Cl}$ angle down from $109.5^{\circ}$ to about $100-107^{\circ}$. Draw P central with one solid wedge, one hashed wedge and one normal bond to Cl, plus a lone pair shown on P to make the pyramid clear.

Final answer: $\text{AlCl}_3$: trigonal planar, bond angle $120^{\circ}$. Diagram shows Al central with three Cl arranged symmetrically in one plane.
$\text{PCl}_3$: trigonal pyramidal, bond angle $100-107^{\circ}$ (accept $107^{\circ}$). Diagram shows P central with three Cl in pyramidal arrangement with lone pair, using wedge / hashed wedge to show 3D.

hints: Use the melting point data, $1074 \text{ K}$ versus $203 \text{ K}$, to decide which chloride has much stronger attractions holding its particles together.
Identify the particle type and lattice for each, ions in a giant lattice versus separate neutral molecules.
Compare what must be broken on melting, strong ionic bonds throughout the lattice versus only weak forces between molecules.
walkthrough:
Picture what SiCl4 really is**
$\text{SiCl}_4$ is covalent and exists as separate, neutral $\text{SiCl}_4$ molecules. There are no ions and no extended lattice. Between these molecules there are only weak London dispersion forces, also called induced dipole-dipole forces or van der Waals forces. Melting only has to loosen these weak attractions, the strong $\text{Si-Cl}$ covalent bonds inside each molecule stay intact.

Picture what NaCl really is**
$\text{NaCl}$ is not molecular at all. It is a giant ionic lattice of $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ ions held in a regular 3D array by strong electrostatic attraction in all directions. To melt it you must break apart these strong ionic bonds so the ions can move freely.

Link strength to melting point**
Strong ionic bonds need a very large amount of thermal energy to break, while weak intermolecular forces need very little. That is why $\text{NaCl}$ melts at $1074 \text{ K}$ and $\text{SiCl}_4$ melts at only $203 \text{ K}$.

Final answer: $\text{SiCl}_4$ is simple molecular with weak van der Waals / London dispersion / induced dipole-dipole forces between molecules.
$\text{NaCl}$ is giant ionic.
Ionic bonding in $\text{NaCl}$ is much stronger than the intermolecular forces in $\text{SiCl}_4$, so much more energy is needed to melt $\text{NaCl}$.

hints: Note that both $\text{SiCl}_4$ and $\text{PCl}_3$ are simple molecular, so focus on what controls the strength of the same type of force between their molecules.
Compare the total number of electrons in one $\text{SiCl}_4$ molecule with one $\text{PCl}_3$ molecule and link this to temporary dipole strength.
walkthrough:
See that both are the same structure type**
Both $\text{SiCl}_4$ and $\text{PCl}_3$ are simple molecular, so melting in both cases only overcomes London dispersion forces between molecules. The difference in melting point must come from a difference in strength of those same forces, not a different bond type.

Use electron count to explain force strength**
$\text{SiCl}_4$ has more electrons per molecule than $\text{PCl}_3$. A larger electron cloud is more easily polarised, so stronger temporary dipoles form. That gives stronger London dispersion forces between $\text{SiCl}_4$ molecules, so more thermal energy is needed to separate them and the melting point is higher ($203 \text{ K}$ versus $161 \text{ K}$).

Final answer: $\text{SiCl}_4$ has more electrons per molecule than $\text{PCl}_3$.
Therefore $\text{SiCl}_4$ has stronger London dispersion / van der Waals forces between molecules, requiring more energy to separate, so higher melting point.

hints: Count outer electrons, Si provides 4 and each Cl provides 7, and plan to show 4 shared pairs around Si with each Cl completing its octet.
walkthrough:
Build the shared octets**
Put Si in the centre. Si has 4 outer electrons to share, one with each Cl. Each Cl has 7 outer electrons, one shared and six as lone pairs. Draw four $\text{Si-Cl}$ bonds, each as a dot from one atom and a cross from the other. Then add three lone pairs on each Cl so every atom is surrounded by 8 electrons. Show outer shell electrons only.

Final answer: Si central with four $\text{Si-Cl}$ single covalent bonds, each bond shown as one dot and one cross. Each Cl has 3 lone pairs to complete octet, Si has octet. Outer electrons only shown.
